October, Instituto Cervantes. Ana is explaining the traps of ser and estar to her adult group. The lorry driver, Mr Costel, has just made a blunder.
Miss, yesterday in Seville I told the waitress the tortilla was very good… and that she was very good too. Why did she go red?
(laughing) Oh, Costel… “La tortilla está buena” means it’s tasty. But “ella está buena” means she’s very attractive. Physically.
Good heavens! I meant to say she’s a good person.
Then you should have said “es muy buena”. With “ser” it’s character. With “estar” it’s something else.
It’s the same with “listo”, isn’t it? “Es listo” is clever, and “está listo” is ready.
Exactly, Ecaterina. For example: “My daughter is clever, but she’s never ready on time.”
And “rico”? In Chile they said the food was “rica”. I thought it was expensive.
Ha-ha. “Ser rico” means having a lot of money. “Estar rico” means being delicious. A dish can be tasty even if it’s cheap.
Well, I’m not rich, but my sarmale are very tasty.
Perfect, Costel! Now a harder one: “Estoy aburrida” and “soy aburrida”.
“Estoy aburrida” is that I’m bored now. “Soy aburrida” is that other people get bored with me.
Very good. And I hope nobody in this class is bored… or boring.
Miss, one more. My son told me yesterday that he’s proud of me. Is that good or bad?
(pauses for a moment) It’s very good, Mr Dan. “Ser orgulloso” means being arrogant, a flaw. But “estar orgulloso de alguien”… is the most beautiful thing a child can say to you.
ree-KEE-see-mo, a-boo-rree-DEE-see-mo: the stress always jumps to “ÍSI”.
“¡Madre mía!” is said with your voice rising a lot on “MEE-a”. It’s the classic reaction to a blunder.
or-goo-YO-so. Context decides: «estoy orgulloso DE ti» (proud) vs «es muy orgulloso» (arrogant).

Es alto. Es médico. Es de Rumanía.
Está cansado. Está en casa. Está roto.
With ordinary adjectives, the difference is just a shade (es guapa / está guapa hoy). But with the adjectives below, the meaning changes completely!
Two famous blunders: “Ella está buena” (= she’s hot, not a good person!). “Él es muy interesado” (= he’s out for himself, not curious!).
You saw the passive with SER (chapter 45): for the action. With ESTAR + participle you describe the RESULT of the action:
La puerta fue cerrada a las diez.
La cena fue preparada por Kenji.
The shop is open until nine.
4. How to describe a complex person
By combining ser and estar, you can say what someone is like in general AND how they are now:
My dad is very serious, but today he’s very cheerful.
She’s a calm person, although lately she’s been on edge.
She’s clever, but she’s still a beginner at maths.
Tip: if you can add “today” or “now” without changing the meaning, it’s estar.
She’s clever, but she’s never ready on time.
My dad is serious, but today he’s cheerful.

Mrs Ecaterina was the most mysterious student in the class. She was eighty, with white hair in a bun and round glasses that kept slipping down her nose. She was very considerate towards everyone, but said little about herself.
The strangest thing was her Spanish. She made beginner’s mistakes with verbs, but then suddenly used words that even Ana didn’t know: “otrora”, “menester”, “acaso”. Words from old books.
One Tuesday, at the end of class, Ecaterina came up to Ana’s desk with a book wrapped in brown paper. “Miss,” she said, “could you tell me whether this translation is well done?”

Ana unwrapped the book. It was an old edition, from the seventies, of García Márquez’s novel “One Hundred Years of Solitude”, translated into Romanian. On the first page, in small letters, it said: “Translation: Ecaterina Ionescu”.
Ana looked up, surprised. “You… you translated this book?”
Ecaterina smiled, a little embarrassed. “Fifty years ago. With a dictionary, a lot of patience and very little Spanish.”
She told her story over a coffee in the institute café. In the seventies, Romania was closed off from the world. You couldn’t travel. Foreign books were banned or censored.
Ecaterina was a young French teacher at the time. A friend secretly lent her a Spanish novel brought by a sailor from Cuba. She didn’t speak Spanish, but she fell in love with the first sentence.
“‘Many years later, in front of the firing squad…’,” she recited softly. “I hardly understood anything. But I knew it was something important. I was sure of it.”

For four years, every evening, after marking French homework, she sat in the kitchen with the book, a French-Spanish dictionary and a French-Romanian one. She translated from Spanish into French and from French into Romanian. Word by word.
“You were very clever,” Ana said admiringly.
“No. I was mad,” Ecaterina answered, and they both burst out laughing. “My husband said I was married to Colonel Aureliano Buendía, not to him.”

When she had finished the translation, she didn’t know what to do with it. No publisher would have published a novel translated by a French teacher who didn’t know Spanish. But a brave editor read it and decided to take the risk.
The book came out in 1976. Fifty thousand copies were sold in a month. For years, it was the only way many Romanians could travel to Macondo.
“And why do you come to A2 classes now?” Ana asked. “You know Spanish better than many Spaniards.”

Ecaterina took off her glasses and slowly wiped them. “No, Miss. I know Spanish from books. I can say ‘menester’ and ‘otrora’. But I’ve never spoken to a Spaniard. I’ve never ordered a coffee in Spanish. I’ve never heard anyone laugh in Spanish in front of me.”
“My husband died last year. Now I’m alone and I have time. And before I die, I want to do something I couldn’t do when I was young.”
“Go to Colombia. See the place where García Márquez was born. And speak to people in their own language, even with mistakes.”
That evening, Ana told Mihai everything. He listened with Rosa Elena asleep in his arms.
“That’s incredible,” said Mihai. “A woman who translated a book without speaking the language.”

“It isn’t incredible,” Ana answered. “It’s what we all do. You translated your grandfather for me for months. I translated my life for my mother. Kenji translated his cooking for us. We’re all translating something, all the time.”

The next day, Ana had an idea. She spoke to the director, Mr Martínez. She suggested organising an event at the Institute: “Romanian translators of Spanish-language literature”. The first guest would be Ecaterina Ionescu.
Mr Martínez was silent for a few seconds. Then he stood up, went to the bookshelf in his office and took down an old book. It was the same edition of “One Hundred Years of Solitude”, in Romanian.
“My first Romanian girlfriend gave me this book in 1985,” he said. “It was the reason I learned Romanian. And, in a way, the reason I’m here.”

“Organise it, Ms García. And tell Mrs Ionescu that if she wants to go to Colombia, the Institute has an exchange programme with Bogotá. She’s retired, but she’s not dead. And from what you tell me, she’s very resourceful.”

Three months later, in January, Mrs Ecaterina got on a plane for the first time in her life. In her suitcase she had her 1976 translation, a very worn dictionary and a letter of recommendation from the Instituto Cervantes.
From Aracataca, García Márquez’s village, she sent Ana a photo. She was standing under an almond tree, in a straw hat, with a huge smile. On the back, someone had written in perfect Spanish:
“Dear Miss: today I ordered a coffee in Spanish. And the waiter told me my accent was very ‘rico’ (tasty). I think he got it right, didn’t he?”
Ana laughed so loudly she woke Rosa Elena. She would have to explain to Ecaterina, very carefully, that accents aren’t “tasty”. But, come to think of it, maybe the waiter was right.
Ecaterina came back from Colombia in February, tanned and ten years younger, according to Costel. The translators’ event finally took place one Thursday in March, in the Institute’s main hall.
The hall was full. There were students, teachers, journalists and lots of men and women her age holding the same old edition of “One Hundred Years of Solitude”. Some had read it four or five times.
Ecaterina was nervous. She had put on her best dress and had spent weeks preparing her speech. But when she went up on stage, she left her notes on the table and spoke without reading.

“For fifty years,” she said, in Spanish, “I thought I had translated a book. But in Colombia I discovered I hadn’t. What I translated was a way of looking at the world. And that way of looking has stayed with me all my life.”
She made three mistakes with verbs. Nobody noticed. Or, if anyone did, they didn’t care. When she finished, the whole hall stood up to applaud her.
In the front row, Mr Dan was clapping harder than anyone. Next to him, Costel whispered in Ana’s ear: “Miss, do you say her speech ‘ha estado muy bueno’ or ‘ha sido muy bueno’?”
Ana smiled. “Both, Costel. This time, both.”

Text to read: The famous blunders
A funny article from the Instituto Cervantes blog.
A student said in class: “Mi profesora está muy buena”. He meant she was a good teacher. The teacher went red and the whole class burst out laughing.
Another student wrote in an exam: “Mi abuelo es muerto”. The correct form is “está muerto”, even though death seems pretty permanent.
A tourist told the doctor: “Soy malo” (I’m a bad person). The doctor answered: “You don’t look it. Are you ill (está usted malo)?”
The moral: with ser and estar, a small mistake can change everything. But relax: Spaniards make mistakes too… in Romanian.
